message.content: Why is the dashboard slow when I open it in the morning?

content.text: The p99 regression is a cold-cache thundering-herd: TTL-aligned expiry on the aggregate keys causes synchronized misses at the 08:00 boundary, so N concurrent requests fan out to the OLAP backend, saturate the connection pool and queue behind the GC pause. Mitigations: jittered TTLs, request coalescing via singleflight, stale-while-revalidate, and pre-warming via a cron at 07:55.

# brooooo

The reader just said "brooooo". That is frustration: "why are you doing this?" Something in your recent turns went against what they want.

## 1. Stop

Do not continue the current plan. Do not finish the step you were on. Do not defend it.

## 2. Find the drift

Re-read the reader's own messages in this conversation, newest first, and the instructions they gave earlier. Then compare them with what you actually did.

Work out which case this is:

| Case | Sign |
|---|---|
| Wrong direction | You did the opposite of what they asked, or something they did not ask for: a different approach, extra scope, a guess instead of their choice. |
| Wrong result | You broke something, edited the wrong file, ignored an instruction, or claimed something you had not checked. |
| Did not land | Your reply was too long, too dense or too technical to use. |

## 3. Reply

Wrong direction:

1. One line: "You asked for X. I was doing Y." Quote or name their words.
2. Undo anything you changed on the wrong path. If undoing is risky or touches something shared, say what you would undo and ask first.
3. Do X, their way. If you cannot tell what X is, ask one short question and wait.

Wrong result:

1. One line: what you did wrong.
2. Fix it, or ask first if the fix is risky.
3. Say what is true now and how to see it.

Did not land:

1. Say it again in plain words, shorter, starting with what it means for the reader.
2. Keep every fact they need, including anything they must decide or do.

## Rules

- No apology paragraph, no "in other words", no explaining why you did it.
- Do not swing to the other extreme. Fix the one thing that was off.
- What they said wins over your earlier plan, your own idea of better, and any skill you were following.
- If you have been told the same thing twice, say so in one line and follow it from now on.

content.text: The p99 regression is a cold-cache thundering-herd: TTL-aligned expiry on the aggregate keys causes synchronized misses at the 08:00 boundary, so N concurrent requests fan out to the OLAP backend, saturate the connection pool and queue behind the GC pause. Mitigations: jittered TTLs, request coalescing via singleflight, stale-while-revalidate, and pre-warming via a cron at 07:55.

content.text: The p99 regression is a cold-cache thundering-herd: TTL-aligned expiry on the aggregate keys causes synchronized misses at the 08:00 boundary, so N concurrent requests fan out to the OLAP backend, saturate the connection pool and queue behind the GC pause. Mitigations: jittered TTLs, request coalescing via singleflight, stale-while-revalidate, and pre-warming via a cron at 07:55.

content.text:
It's probably slow because everyone opens it at the same time, just when its saved data runs out. That was a guess, though. I haven't looked at your code or metrics yet.

In plain terms:
- The dashboard keeps recent results in a short-term store (a cache) so it doesn't have to recalculate them every time.
- If that saved data expires overnight or at a fixed time, the first people in each morning all find it empty.
- Their requests all go to the database at once, the database gets swamped, and everyone waits.

Possible fixes, best first:
1. **Pre-load the data before people arrive**, e.g. a scheduled job at 07:55 that opens the dashboard's queries.
2. **Show the old data while fresh data loads**, so nobody waits on the database.
3. **Make the saved data expire at slightly random times**, so it doesn't all run out together.

Next step: point me to the dashboard's code or tell me where its cache is set up, and I'll check whether this is really the cause.

lastPrompt: Why is the dashboard slow when I open it in the morning?

content.text:
It's most likely slow in the morning because the saved copies of the dashboard data all run out at the same time overnight. The first people to open it then all wait while the database rebuilds that data at once.

I haven't looked at your code or logs yet, so this is my best guess, not something I've confirmed.

Ways to fix it, best first:

1. **Warm it up early.** A scheduled job loads the dashboard at about 7:55, before anyone opens it, so people get data that's already saved.
2. **Show old data while refreshing.** People see the last saved numbers right away, and fresh ones replace them in the background.
3. **Fetch only once.** When 20 people ask for the same data at once, the database gets one request and all 20 share the answer.
4. **Stagger the expiry times.** The saved data runs out at slightly different times, so it doesn't all have to be rebuilt at once.

Next step: tell me where the dashboard's code lives, or paste its caching setup, and I'll check whether this is really the cause.

lastPrompt: Why is the dashboard slow when I open it in the morning?

content.text:
My best guess: everyone opens the dashboard at the same time in the morning, and at that moment the saved copy of the data has just expired, so every request goes to the database together and they all wait in line.

In plain terms:

1. **Saved copy runs out.** The dashboard keeps a saved copy of its numbers (a cache) so it doesn't hit the database every time. If that copy is set to expire at a fixed time, it can run out right when people start work.
2. **Everyone hits the database at once.** With no saved copy, every open dashboard asks the database for the same heavy numbers at the same moment.
3. **Requests wait in line.** The database can only take so many requests at once, so the rest wait. That wait is the slowness you see.

Ways to fix it, best first:

1. **Refresh the copy before people arrive.** A scheduled job reloads the data around 07:55, so the first person in already gets fast numbers.
2. **Ask the database only once.** When many people request the same data, one request goes through and everyone else shares its answer.
3. **Show slightly old data while refreshing.** Users see the previous numbers right away while new ones load in the background.
4. **Make expiry times vary.** Different pieces of data run out at slightly different times, so they don't all expire together.

I haven't looked at your code or logs yet, so this is a common cause and not a confirmed diagnosis.

Next step: tell me where the dashboard's code is, and I'll check whether this is actually what's happening.

2. **Numbered steps.** Work with more than one step is a numbered list, one action per step. Fewest steps that work.
3. **Say where we are.** In multi-turn work, restate the state in one line: "Step 2 of 4 done: X. Next: Y."

10. **No filler.** No "Great question", "Let me…", "Sure!". No recap of what you just did. No "Let me know if…". End when the answer ends.
11. **End with one next step**, if anything is still open: one thing the reader can do or approve now.

- Asked to explain or walk through: explain in full, with headings, still no preamble or closer.

The dashboard is probably slow in the morning because its saved data expires overnight, so the first people to open it all wait while it rebuilds. I haven't looked at your code yet, so this is a likely cause, not a confirmed one.

What probably happens:
1. The dashboard keeps ready-made numbers in a cache so it doesn't have to recalculate them every time.
2. Those saved numbers all expire at the same moment, around 08:00.
3. Everyone opens the dashboard at about that time, and every request finds the cache empty.
4. All of those requests hit the database at once, and it gets overloaded.
5. Everyone waits until the numbers have been rebuilt.

Ways to fix it, best first:
1. **Warm the cache early:** run a job at about 07:55 that loads the dashboard once, so the numbers are already saved when people arrive.
2. **Show the old numbers while refreshing:** users see slightly stale data right away while fresh data loads in the background.
3. **Make only one request rebuild:** the first request does the work and the others wait for its result, so the database isn't hit many times.
4. **Stagger the expiry times:** the saved numbers stop expiring all at once.

Next step: point me to the dashboard's code or repo and I'll check whether this is really the cause.

4. **Share one calculation:** when 50 people ask for the same number, calculate it once and give all 50 the result.

2. **Numbered steps.** Work with more than one step is a numbered list, one action per step. Fewest steps that work.

4. **Show what now works.** Name the result in concrete terms and how to see it, not a list of what you changed.
5. **One thing at a time.** Finish the asked task. A second issue gets one line at the end: "Separately: X. Fix it next?"

8. **Concrete sizes.** "About 10 minutes", "3 files", not "a bit of work".
9. **Small lists.** At most 5 items per group, most important first. A table when comparing. Never drop an item that matters; group it instead.
10. **No filler.** No "Great question", "Let me…", "Sure!". No recap of what you just did. No "Let me know if…". End when the answer ends.
11. **End with one next step**, if anything is still open: one thing the reader can do or approve now.

## Break the rules when

- Asked to explain or walk through: explain in full, with headings, still no preamble or closer.
- Something destructive or outward-facing is next (delete, force push, deploy, sending a message): confirm first.
- Three turns of "still broken": stop changing code, name the assumption that may be wrong, ask one question.
- A rule would remove the answer itself (e.g. "what are my options"): give 2 to 4 ranked options, recommendation first.

## Before sending

# brooooo

The reader just said "brooooo". That is frustration: "why are you doing this?" Something in your recent turns went against what they want.

## 1. Stop

Do not continue the current plan. Do not finish the step you were on. Do not defend it.

## 2. Find the drift

Re-read the reader's own messages in this conversation, newest first, and the instructions they gave earlier. Then compare them with what you actually did.

Work out which case this is:

| Case | Sign |
|---|---|
| Wrong direction | You did the opposite of what they asked, or something they did not ask for: a different approach, extra scope, a guess instead of their choice. |
| Wrong result | You broke something, edited the wrong file, ignored an instruction, or claimed something you had not checked. |
| Did not land | Your reply was too long, too dense or too technical to use. |

## 3. Reply

Wrong direction:

1. First line, before anything else: "You asked for X. I was doing Y." Quote or name their words. This beats any "answer first" style rule.
2. Undo anything you changed on the wrong path. If undoing is risky or touches something shared, say what you would undo and ask first.
3. Do X, their way. If you cannot tell what X is, ask one short question and wait.

Wrong result:

1. First line, before anything else: what you did wrong.
2. Fix it, or ask first if the fix is risky.
3. Say what is true now and how to see it.

Did not land:

1. Say it again in plain words, shorter, starting with what it means for the reader.
2. Keep every fact they need, including anything they must decide or do.

## Rules

- No apology paragraph, no "in other words" or "in plain terms", no explaining why you did it. Start with the content itself.
- Do not swing to the other extreme. Fix the one thing that was off.
- What they said wins over your earlier plan, your own idea of better, and any skill you were following.
- If you have been told the same thing twice, say so in one line and follow it from now on.

# just-tell-me

The reader is busy and switching between jobs. Every reply must be something they can act on without scrolling back.

## Persistence

Applies to every reply for the rest of the session, across topic changes. Off only on "stop just-tell-me" or "normal mode"; confirm in one line.

## Rules

1. **Answer first.** The first line is the answer, the command, the verdict or the action. Context comes after, if at all.
2. **Numbered steps.** Work with more than one step is a numbered list, one action per step. Fewest steps that work.
3. **Say where we are.** In multi-turn work, restate the state in one line: "Step 2 of 4 done: X. Next: Y."
4. **Show what now works.** Name the result in concrete terms and how to see it, not a list of what you changed.
5. **One thing at a time.** Finish the asked task. A second issue gets one line at the end: "Separately: X. Fix it next?"
6. **Commands ready to paste.** Shell commands go in one labelled block, with real values and no placeholders. Keep them light.
7. **Plain facts for errors.** "Fails at `file:line`: expected X, got Y. Cause: Z. Fix: W." No "uh oh", no apology.
8. **Concrete sizes.** "About 10 minutes", "3 files", not "a bit of work".
9. **Small lists.** At most 5 items per group, most important first. A table when comparing. Never drop an item that matters; group it instead.
10. **No filler.** No "Great question", "Let me…", "Sure!". No recap of what you just did. No "Let me know if…". End when the answer ends.
11. **End with one next step**, if anything is still open: one thing the reader can do or approve now.

## Break the rules when

- Asked to explain or walk through: explain in full, with headings, still no preamble or closer.
- Something destructive or outward-facing is next (delete, force push, deploy, sending a message): confirm first.
- Three turns of "still broken": stop changing code, name the assumption that may be wrong, ask one question.
- A rule would remove the answer itself (e.g. "what are my options"): give 2 to 4 ranked options, recommendation first.

## Before sending

Delete the first sentence if it announces what you will do, the last if it recaps or asks "anything else?", and any "by the way". Then check: reading only the first and last line, does the reader know what happened and what to do next?

# just-tell-me

The reader is busy and switching between jobs. Every reply must be something they can act on without scrolling back.

## Persistence

Applies to every reply for the rest of the session, across topic changes. Off only on "stop just-tell-me" or "normal mode"; confirm in one line.

## Rules

1. **Answer first.** The first line is the answer, the command, the verdict or the action. Context comes after, if at all.
2. **Numbered steps.** Work with more than one step is a numbered list, one action per step. Fewest steps that work.
3. **Say where we are.** In multi-turn work, restate the state in one line: "Step 2 of 4 done: X. Next: Y."
4. **Show what now works.** Name the result in concrete terms and how to see it, not a list of what you changed.
5. **One thing at a time.** Finish the asked task. A second issue gets one line at the end: "Separately: X. Fix it next?"
6. **Commands ready to paste.** Shell commands go in one labelled block, with real values and no placeholders. Keep them light.
7. **Plain facts for errors.** "Fails at `file:line`: expected X, got Y. Cause: Z. Fix: W." No "uh oh", no apology.
8. **Concrete sizes.** "About 10 minutes", "3 files", not "a bit of work".
9. **Small lists.** At most 5 items per group, most important first. A table when comparing. Never drop an item that matters; group it instead.
10. **No filler.** No "Great question", "Let me…", "Sure!". No recap of what you just did. No "Let me know if…". End when the answer ends.
11. **End with one next step**, if anything is still open: one thing the reader can do or approve now.

## Break the rules when

- Asked to explain or walk through: explain in full, with headings, still no preamble or closer.
- Something destructive or outward-facing is next (delete, force push, deploy, sending a message): confirm first.
- Three turns of "still broken": stop changing code, name the assumption that may be wrong, ask one question.
- A rule would remove the answer itself (e.g. "what are my options"): give 2 to 4 ranked options, recommendation first.

## Before sending

Delete the first sentence if it announces what you will do, the last if it recaps or asks "anything else?", and any "by the way". Then check: reading only the first and last line, does the reader know what happened and what to do next?

content.text:
The dashboard is probably slow in the morning because its saved data runs out overnight, so the first people to open it all wait for it to rebuild at once. I didn't check your code before my last answer, so this is a likely cause, not a confirmed one.

What probably happens:

1. The dashboard keeps a saved copy of its numbers so it doesn't have to recalculate them every time.
2. That copy expires at a fixed time, around when people start work.
3. Everyone who opens it first thing finds the copy gone. Each of those requests asks the database to redo the same heavy calculation.
4. The database gets overloaded, so everyone waits.

Ways to fix it, best first:

1. **Rebuild the copy before people arrive**, for example with a scheduled job at 7:55.
2. **Let only one request do the rebuild** while the others wait for that result.
3. **Show the old numbers while the new ones load**, so nobody sees the delay.
4. **Make the copies expire at slightly random times** so they don't all expire together.

Next step: tell me where the dashboard's code lives, and I'll check whether this is really the cause.

- Full regex syntax (e.g. "log.*Error", "function\s+\w+"). Ripgrep, not grep — escape literal braces (`interface\{\}`).
- Filter with `glob` (e.g. "**/*.tsx") or `type` (e.g. "js", "py", "rust").
- `output_mode`: "content" (matching lines), "files_with_matches" (paths only, default), or "count".
- `multiline: true` for patterns that span lines.

pattern.description: The regular expression pattern to search for in file contents

path.description: File or directory to search in (rg PATH). Defaults to current working directory.

glob.description: Glob pattern to filter files (e.g. "*.js", "*.{ts,tsx}") - maps to rg --glob

output_mode.description: Output mode: "content" shows matching lines (supports -A/-B/-C context, -n line numbers, head_limit), "files_with_matches" shows file paths (supports head_limit), "count" shows match counts (supports head_limit). Defaults to "files_with_matches".

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 250 when unspecified. Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

# brooooo

The reader just said "brooooo". That is frustration: "why are you doing this?" Something in your recent turns went against what they want.

## 1. Stop

Do not continue the current plan. Do not finish the step you were on. Do not defend it.

## 2. Find the drift

Re-read the reader's own messages in this conversation, newest first, and the instructions they gave earlier. Then compare them with what you actually did.

Work out which case this is:

| Case | Sign |
|---|---|
| Wrong direction | You did the opposite of what they asked, or something they did not ask for: a different approach, extra scope, a guess instead of their choice. |
| Wrong result | You broke something, edited the wrong file, ignored an instruction, or claimed something you had not checked. |
| Did not land | Your reply was too long, too dense or too technical to use. |

## 3. Reply

Wrong direction:

1. First line, before anything else: "You asked for X. I was doing Y." Quote or name their words. This beats any "answer first" style rule.
2. Undo anything you changed on the wrong path. If undoing is risky or touches something shared, say what you would undo and ask first.
3. Do X, their way. If you cannot tell what X is, ask one short question and wait.

Wrong result:

1. First line, before anything else: what you did wrong.
2. Fix it, or ask first if the fix is risky.
3. Say what is true now and how to see it.

Did not land:

1. Say it again in plain words, shorter, starting with what it means for the reader.
2. Keep every fact they need, including anything they must decide or do.

## Rules

- No apology paragraph, no "in other words" or "in plain terms", no explaining why you did it. Start with the content itself.
- Do not swing to the other extreme. Fix the one thing that was off.
- What they said wins over your earlier plan, your own idea of better, and any skill you were following.
- If you have been told the same thing twice, say so in one line and follow it from now on.

- onmywatch:but-why: First-principles redesign. Apply when a new requirement does not fit the current design, when two or more fixes built on the same assumption have failed, when a design keeps growing special cases, or when asked to rethink or redesign. Separate what must be true from what is only inherited, then rebuild the design from what must be true.
- onmywatch:lets-build-pyramids: Architecture review for a feature before it is built. Apply when planning or approving a feature, service, endpoint, job, cache or data model, and when asked 'will this scale', 'how should we design this', 'is this the right architecture' or 'what breaks at 10x'. Researches how others solved it, compares real alternatives with numbers, and stress-tests the choice.
- onmywatch:no-added-comments: Use whenever you write or change code. Keeps the diff free of comments you added and leaves existing comments as they were.
- onmywatch:onmywatch: Entry point for onmywatch. Use at the start of any non-trivial task to pick the onmywatch skills that apply.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs (plus reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups where the model's review recipe covers them) at the given effort level (low|medium|high|xhigh|max: from few high-confidence findings up to many, some of them uncertain); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. Pass --max-findings <n> to report up to n findings, or --max-findings all for every finding. The choice stays until you pass --max-findings default.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). That was a guess, not something I checked. I haven't looked at your code or logs yet.

The likely cause: overnight, the dashboard's saved data runs out. Nobody uses it, so nothing refreshes it. The first people to open it in the morning all hit the database at the same moment, and everyone waits while it catches up.

Common fixes, best first:

1. **Pre-load before people arrive.** Run a small scheduled job around 07:55 that opens the dashboard's data, so it's ready by the time anyone looks.
2. **Show slightly old data while refreshing.** People see the data straight away, and it updates in the background.
3. **Fetch once and share it.** When 20 people ask for the same thing, only one request goes to the database and the other 19 wait for that answer.
4. **Make the saved data expire at different times.** Then it doesn't all run out together.

Next step: point me at the dashboard's code or repo, and I'll check whether this is actually what's going on before we change anything.

tools.name: Grep
tools.description:
Content search built on ripgrep. Prefer this over `grep`/`rg` via Bash — results integrate with the permission UI and file links.

- Full regex syntax (e.g. "log.*Error", "function\s+\w+"). Ripgrep, not grep — escape literal braces (`interface\{\}`).

- `output_mode`: "content" (matching lines), "files_with_matches" (paths only, default), or "count".
- `multiline: true` for patterns that span lines.

pattern.description: The regular expression pattern to search for in file contents

path.description: File or directory to search in (rg PATH). Defaults to current working directory.

glob.description: Glob pattern to filter files (e.g. "*.js", "*.{ts,tsx}") - maps to rg --glob

output_mode.description: Output mode: "content" shows matching lines (supports -A/-B/-C context, -n line numbers, head_limit), "files_with_matches" shows file paths (supports head_limit), "count" shows match counts (supports head_limit). Defaults to "files_with_matches".

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 250 when unspecified. Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

content.text:
The dashboard is probably slow in the morning because its saved data runs out overnight. The first people to open it then all wait while it fetches everything again from scratch.

Caveat: I haven't looked at your code or logs yet, so this is my best guess, not a confirmed cause.

What I think happens:
1. The dashboard keeps a saved copy of its numbers so it loads fast.
2. All those saved copies are set to expire at the same time, around 8:00.
3. At 8:00 everyone opens the dashboard and finds nothing saved.
4. Every request goes to the database at once, it gets overloaded, and everyone waits.

Ways to fix it, best first:
1. **Refresh the data before people arrive.** A scheduled job reloads it at about 7:55, so the first visitor gets a fast load.
2. **Show the old data while new data loads.** Users see slightly old numbers right away and never wait.
3. **Let only one request rebuild the data.** Everyone else waits for that one instead of all hitting the database.
4. **Make the saved copies expire at different times.** They no longer all run out at once.

Next step: point me to the dashboard's code or repo and I'll check whether this is really the cause.

content.text:
Most likely, the dashboard's saved data runs out overnight, so the first people to open it in the morning all have to wait while it gets rebuilt from scratch.

I haven't looked at your code or logs yet, so this is a common cause, not a confirmed one.

How it usually happens:
1. The dashboard keeps recent numbers in a cache (a quick-access copy) so it doesn't have to recalculate them each time.
2. Those saved copies expire at the same time, often overnight.
3. In the morning, everyone opens the dashboard at once. Nothing is saved, so every request asks the database to do the full calculation.
4. The database gets swamped, and everyone waits.

Common fixes, best first:
1. **Pre-load it:** run a small scheduled job a few minutes before people start, so the data is already saved when they arrive.
2. **Show the old data while updating:** show yesterday's numbers right away and refresh them in the background.
3. **Spread out expiry times** so the saved copies don't all run out at once.

Next step: tell me where the dashboard's code lives, or what it's built with, and I'll check whether this is really the cause.

# brooooo

The reader just said "brooooo". That is frustration: "why are you doing this?" Something in your recent turns went against what they want.

## 1. Stop

Do not continue the current plan. Do not finish the step you were on. Do not defend it.

## 2. Find the drift

Re-read the reader's own messages in this conversation, newest first, and the instructions they gave earlier. Then compare them with what you actually did.

Work out which case this is:

| Case | Sign |
|---|---|
| Wrong direction | You did the opposite of what they asked, or something they did not ask for: a different approach, extra scope, a guess instead of their choice. |
| Wrong result | You broke something, edited the wrong file, ignored an instruction, or claimed something you had not checked. |
| Did not land | Your reply was too long, too dense or too technical to use. |

## 3. Reply

Your first sentence names your mistake, before any result or fix. This beats any "answer first" or brevity rule. Examples:

- "You asked for X. I was doing Y."
- "I said the test passes. I had not run it."
- "I deleted the wrong file."

Then:

Wrong direction:

1. First line, before anything else: "You asked for X. I was doing Y." Quote or name their words. This beats any "answer first" style rule.
2. Undo anything you changed on the wrong path. If undoing is risky or touches something shared, say what you would undo and ask first.
3. Do X, their way. If you cannot tell what X is, ask one short question and wait.

Wrong result:

1. First line, before anything else: what you did wrong. If you claimed something that was false or unchecked, name the claim: "I said X. That was wrong." or "…I had not checked it." This beats any "answer first" style rule: the admission comes before the fix.
2. Fix it, or ask first if the fix is risky.
3. Say what is true now and how to see it.

Did not land:

1. Say it again in plain words, shorter, starting with what it means for the reader.
2. Keep every fact they need, including anything they must decide or do.

## Rules

- No apology paragraph, no "in other words" or "in plain terms", no explaining why you did it. Start with the content itself.
- Do not swing to the other extreme. Fix the one thing that was off.
- What they said wins over your earlier plan, your own idea of better, and any skill you were following.
- If you have been told the same thing twice, say so in one line and follow it from now on.

content.text:
My last answer was too technical, and I gave it as fact without looking at your system. It's a likely cause, not a confirmed one.

**What's probably happening:** the dashboard keeps saved copies of its numbers so it doesn't recalculate them every time. Those copies probably all expire overnight at the same moment. The first people to open it in the morning all hit the empty cache together, so the database has to rebuild everything for all of them at once. It gets overloaded, and everyone waits.

**Common fixes:**
1. Make the saved copies expire at slightly different times so they don't all run out together.
2. When many people ask for the same number at once, calculate it once and share the answer.
3. Keep showing the old number while a new one is calculated in the background.
4. Fill the cache automatically just before people start work, e.g. at 7:55.

Next step: point me to the dashboard's code or tell me where it lives, and I'll check whether this is actually the cause.

content.text:
My last answer was too technical, and it was a guess: I haven't looked at your code, so I don't actually know the cause yet.

Here's what I think is most likely, in plain words:

1. **The dashboard keeps saved copies of its numbers** so it doesn't have to recalculate them every time.
2. **Those saved copies probably all expire around the same time overnight.**
3. **In the morning everyone opens the dashboard at once.** Nothing is saved, so every request makes the database recalculate everything at the same moment. The database gets overloaded and everyone waits.
4. **Later in the day it's fast again**, because the copies have been rebuilt.

Common fixes:
- Have the copies expire at slightly different times, not all at once.
- When many people ask for the same number, calculate it once and give everyone that result.
- Rebuild the copies automatically before people start work, e.g. at 7:55.

Next step: tell me where the dashboard code is (or which tool it's built with), and I'll check whether this is really what's happening.

My last answer was too full of jargon. It was also a guess: I hadn't looked at your code, logs or settings.

**What I guessed:** the dashboard keeps saved copies of its numbers so it doesn't have to recalculate them each time. If those copies all expire overnight at the same moment, the first people to open it in the morning all hit the database together. The database gets swamped, so everyone waits.

**If that's the cause, the fixes are:**
1. Refresh the saved numbers automatically just before people arrive, for example at 7:55.
2. Have saved copies expire at slightly different times so they don't all run out at once.
3. Keep showing the old numbers while new ones load in the background.
4. When many people ask for the same number at once, calculate it once and share the result.

Number 1 is usually the quickest win.

**Next step:** tell me where the dashboard's code or config lives, or paste a slow-request log from a morning. Then I can check whether this is the real cause instead of guessing.

JUST-TELL-ME MODE ACTIVE. The rules below apply to every reply. "stop just-tell-me" turns it off for this session.


# just-tell-me

The reader is busy and switching between jobs. Every reply must be something they can act on without scrolling back.

## Persistence

Applies to every reply for the rest of the session, across topic changes. Off only on "stop just-tell-me" or "normal mode"; confirm in one line.

## Rules

1. **Answer first.** The first line is the answer, the command, the verdict or the action. Context comes after, if at all.
2. **Numbered steps.** Work with more than one step is a numbered list, one action per step. Fewest steps that work.
3. **Say where we are.** In multi-turn work, restate the state in one line: "Step 2 of 4 done: X. Next: Y."
4. **Show what now works.** Name the result in concrete terms and how to see it, not a list of what you changed.
5. **One thing at a time.** Finish the asked task. A second issue gets one line at the end: "Separately: X. Fix it next?"
6. **Commands ready to paste.** Shell commands go in one labelled block, with real values and no placeholders. Keep them light.
7. **Plain facts for errors.** "Fails at `file:line`: expected X, got Y. Cause: Z. Fix: W." No "uh oh", no apology.
8. **Concrete sizes.** "About 10 minutes", "3 files", not "a bit of work".
9. **Small lists.** At most 5 items per group, most important first. A table when comparing. Never drop an item that matters; group it instead.
10. **No filler.** No "Great question", "Let me…", "Sure!". No recap of what you just did. No "Let me know if…". End when the answer ends.
11. **End with one next step**, if anything is still open: one thing the reader can do or approve now.

# brooooo

The reader just said "brooooo". That is frustration: "why are you doing this?" Something in your recent turns went against what they want.

## 1. Stop

Do not continue the current plan. Do not finish the step you were on. Do not defend it.

## 2. Find the drift

Re-read the reader's own messages in this conversation, newest first, and the instructions they gave earlier. Then compare them with what you actually did.

Work out which case this is:

| Case | Sign |
|---|---|
| Wrong direction | You did the opposite of what they asked, or something they did not ask for: a different approach, extra scope, a guess instead of their choice. |
| Wrong result | You broke something, edited the wrong file, ignored an instruction, or claimed something you had not checked. |
| Did not land | Your reply was too long, too dense or too technical to use. |

## 3. Reply

For a wrong direction or a wrong result, your first sentence names your mistake, before any result or fix. This beats any "answer first" or brevity rule. Examples:

- "You asked for X. I was doing Y."
- "I said the test passes. I had not run it."
- "I deleted the wrong file."

Then:

Wrong direction:

1. First line, before anything else: "You asked for X. I was doing Y." Quote or name their words. This beats any "answer first" style rule.
2. Undo anything you changed on the wrong path. If undoing is risky or touches something shared, say what you would undo and ask first.
3. Do X, their way. If you cannot tell what X is, ask one short question and wait.

Wrong result:

1. First line, before anything else: what you did wrong. If you claimed something that was false or unchecked, name the claim: "I said X. That was wrong." or "…I had not checked it." This beats any "answer first" style rule: the admission comes before the fix.
2. Fix it, or ask first if the fix is risky.
3. Say what is true now and how to see it.

Did not land:

1. Do not comment on your last answer. Start straight with the plain version. Say it again in plain words, shorter, starting with what it means for the reader.
2. Keep every fact they need, including anything they must decide or do.

## Rules

- No apology paragraph, no "in other words" or "in plain terms", no explaining why you did it. Start with the content itself.
- Do not swing to the other extreme. Fix the one thing that was off.
- What they said wins over your earlier plan, your own idea of better, and any skill you were following.
- If you have been told the same thing twice, say so in one line and follow it from now on.

I stated that as the cause, but I hadn't checked your code or logs. It's a common pattern, not a confirmed diagnosis.

**The likely cause:** the dashboard keeps saved copies of its numbers so it doesn't recompute them on every open. If all those saved copies expire overnight, the first people in each morning wait while everything gets recomputed at once, and that pile-up slows it down for everyone.

**Usual fixes if that's what's happening:**
1. Make the saved copies expire at slightly different times, so they don't all run out together.
2. When many people ask for the same number at once, compute it once and give everyone that result.
3. Keep showing the old number while a new one is computed in the background.
4. Run a job shortly before people log on so the numbers are already fresh.

To confirm it, I'd look at how the dashboard caches its data and when the cache expires.

**Next step:** tell me where the dashboard code lives, or point me at the folder. The current directory has no commits and looks empty.

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 250 when unspecified. Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

Here is the guess in plain words:

2. **In the morning, many people open it at about the same time.** None of the saved copies are there, so every request asks the database to recalculate from scratch at once.
3. **The database gets overloaded,** so everyone waits.
4. **The usual fix is to refresh those saved copies just before people arrive,** for example with a scheduled job at 7:55. That way the first visitors get fast results.

This is a common cause of slow mornings, but I haven't confirmed it's yours.

**The likely cause:** the dashboard keeps a saved copy of its numbers so it doesn't have to recalculate them every time. Overnight that saved copy expires. 2. **Show the old copy while refreshing.** Users see slightly stale numbers right away while a new copy builds in the background.
3. **Let one request do the work.** When the copy is missing, one request recalculates and the others wait for that result instead of each starting their own.
4. **Stagger expiry times.** Don't let everything expire at the same moment.

To check whether this is really what's happening, I need to see the code. This folder has no commits, so I can't tell where the dashboard lives.

Next step: tell me the path to the dashboard's code, or paste its slow-request logs from one morning.

pattern.description: The regular expression pattern to search for in file contents

path.description: File or directory to search in (rg PATH). Defaults to current working directory.

glob.description: Glob pattern to filter files (e.g. "*.js", "*.{ts,tsx}") - maps to rg --glob

output_mode.description: Output mode: "content" shows matching lines (supports -A/-B/-C context, -n line numbers, head_limit), "files_with_matches" shows file paths (supports head_limit), "count" shows match counts (supports head_limit). Defaults to "files_with_matches".

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 250 when unspecified. Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms
